title: Allocate Marginal Reviews to Borderline Papers Using LLM Comparative Ranking
claim: Rank items by LLM pairwise comparison to find the borderline band, then shift the same review budget toward it.
layout: 2 stacked rows: 3-box flow on top, 2 side-by-side panels below
description: The figure is titled 'Marginal Review Allocation' and has two stacked stages. The top section, 'Step 1: Identify likely borderline papers', is three boxes in a row. The first is 'Submitted papers' (Paper 1, 2, ..., N). The second is 'LLM pairwise comparisons' (Paper 1 vs Paper 2, and so on). The third is 'Comparative ranking', a ranked list with colored bands: green for likely accept, grey for the borderline region, pink for likely reject. A dashed line marks the acceptance cutoff. The bottom section, 'Step 2: Allocate human reviewers', has two side-by-side boxes. 'Typical practice' shows 3.3 average reviewers per paper in every band. 'Proposed allocation (ours)' shows 3, 4 and 3, with the borderline 4 in bold. A footer reads 'Same total reviewers • Better placement'. The eye goes first to the colored bands and the bold 4.
caption: Schematic of the marginal review allocation pipeline. Step 1 uses LLM pairwise comparisons to construct a comparative ranking and identify a borderline band around the acceptance percentile. Step 2 allocates marginal reviews to that band while keeping total reviewer load fixed, with numbers shown for illustration.
abstract: This paper argues that large ML conferences should allocate marginal review capacity primarily to papers near the acceptance boundary, rather than spreading extra reviews via random or affinity-driven heuristics. We propose using LLM-based comparative ranking (via pairwise comparisons and a Bradley--Terry model) to identify a borderline band \emph{before} human reviewing and to allocate \emph{marginal} reviewer capacity at assignment time. Concretely, given a venue-specific minimum review target (e.g., 3 or 4), we use this signal to decide which papers receive one additional review (e.g., a 4th or 5th), without conditioning on any human reviews and without using LLM outputs for accept/reject. We provide a simple expected-impact calculation in terms of (i) the overlap between the predicted and true borderline sets ($Ï$) and (ii) the incremental value of an extra review near the boundary ($Î$), and we provide retrospective proxies to estimate these quantities.
